title: Spending and saving: needs and wants

accuracy.evidence: Checked on 24 Nov 2026 against the PSHE Association Programme of Study (2020) KS1 Living in the wider world L10-L13 (what money is; people choose how to save and spend; the difference between needs and wants and that people may not always have what they want; money needs looking after), and MoneyHelper's Financial education planning framework 3-11 (needs before wants, saving over time, keeping money safe). The needs listed (food, water, a home, warm clothes, medicine) are the standard KS1 examples; the adult text notes that some things can be either. All sums are exact in whole pounds: 2+1+2 = 5 of 10 leaves 5, less than the 8 pound robot; 5 weeks of 2 pounds is the 10 pound kite; 3+2 = 5 uses the 5 pounds and leaves out the 4 pound ball.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented KS1 money slips named in PSHE and MoneyHelper guidance: 'I really want it, so it is a need' (step 1 prediction and the special Sweets refusal), buying wants first and running short (step 2 prediction; the refusal tells the child to put a want back because needs come first), spent money comes back (sweet-shop message 'it does not come back'), small savings are pointless ('save' slip), leaving money where it can be lost (three unsafe places with reasons), and expecting to have every want (step 5 refuses the ball once the comic is chosen, 'all' slip).

lab_distinct.evidence: Five money mechanisms of this topic: a draggable need-or-want card sorter, a 10 pound shop with a basket total and a refusal that names the missing needs, a weekly save-or-spend choice filling a jar to a 10 pound kite line, a safe-places finder, and a 5 pound wants chooser that names what was given up. It is not the living-things flagneeds lab (survival needs of animals and plants) nor the maths money labs (coin values, change). The gate measured under 30% source overlap with every other flag_*.js.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each idea is met by doing it before the strip confirms it: the Sweets card bounces out of Need; putting the robot in first means the milk is refused for lack of money; spending on sweets adds a week but nothing to the jar; the bench and holey pocket are refused with how money gets lost; and after choosing the comic and stickers the ball cannot be bought, so the child feels the trade-off.

predictions.evidence: Two committed predictions with tempting wrong options: 'Are sweets a need?' (tempting: yes, I really want them), disproved when the Sweets card is refused from Need; and 'You have 10 pounds; bread, milk and apples cost 5 and the robot is 8; can you buy it all?' (tempting: yes, 10 pounds is lots), disproved when the basket cannot take everything. Tasks cannot complete until a prediction is locked, and the done message names it.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Eight challenge questions; each wrong option carries a tagged slip with its own message: 'want' (wanting a lot is not needing), 'need' (a winter coat keeps us well), 'first' (needs before wants or no money for food), 'gone' (spent money does not come back), 'save' (2 pounds for 3 weeks is 6), 'safe' (bench or holey pocket loses money), 'all' (money runs out, so choosing one means going without another).

readability.evidence: Kid text uses one- and two-syllable words and short sentences (need, want, save, spend, money box); validate_lessons.py passed the kid and adult readability limits. Lab strips are one short sentence, prices are whole pounds within Year 1 and Year 2 number, and buttons say exactly what they do (Buy bread £2, Save £2).

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph teaches one idea (need vs want; needs first; saving and spent money; choosing between wants). Adult paragraphs give the PSHE codes, the definitions with the 'can be either' caveat, the mistakes and what the lab does; the content gate found no filler phrases and under 12% overlap with any other lesson, including Money basics: budgeting and saving.

mobile.evidence: Checked on iPhone 13 screenshots in dark and light themes for every step after Show me: the young-class buttons are 56 px tall, the shop grid drops to three columns with prices readable, the basket label sits above its bar, the jar, kite and sweets cards fit side by side, the six places fit in two columns, and nothing is clipped.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin (Need and Want naming the card; Buy or Put back with price; Save 2 pounds and Spend 2 pounds on sweets; each place; each want with price). Drag is optional. The canvas aria-label follows every message, the challenge feedback is a polite live region, and walk.cjs found axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13 with no console errors.

sources: PSHE Association, Programme of Study for PSHE Education Key Stages 1-5 (2020), KS1 Living in the wider world L10-L13
MoneyHelper (Money and Pensions Service), Financial education planning framework 3-11
Whitebread, D. and Bingham, S. (2013) Habit formation and learning in young children, Money Advice Service
